fetched_contents.text: Secondary headaches - red and green flags and their significance for diagnostics Abstract A small percentage of patients suffer from a secondary headache syndrome. It is imperative that clinicians are able to differentiate primary headache syndromes from secondary headache syndromes, as failure to do so significantly worsens morbidity and mortality. Recent advances in our understanding of pathobiological mechanisms offer useful information on these enigmatic disorders. We now understand that the causes of secondary headache syndromes can vary significantly – these may be infectious, inflammatory, vascular, traumatic or structural in origin. A well-taken history and targeted physical examination coupled with appropriate investigations can enable these syndromes to be recognized consistently and thus allow their timely and appropriate treatment. Along with their epidemiology, some of their key characteristics shall thus be discussed in this review so as to aid the busy clinician at the bedside. Red flags including sudden onset, high pain intensity, pattern of change of a preexisting headache, focal neurological signs or seizure, systemic signs and precipitation by physical activity can guide the clinician to suspect a secondary headache. Importantly a preexisting headache is not an exclusion of a secondary headache – it might even be a predisposition in certain cases. Keywords: Headache, SNOOP-10, SNOOP-12, Secondary headache 1. Introduction Headaches are generally divided into primary and secondary headache disorders, where primary headaches such as migraine or cluster headaches are the disease itself, whereas secondary headaches are the expression of an underlying disease. The epidemiology of secondary headaches may vary depending on the clinical setting or the population sampled. For example, emergency-based studies yielded a prevalence rate of 2% to 7% [1,2] while the numbers documented in community-based research ranges from 2% to 23% [3,4]. Age-related variability may also be observed, with elderly patients having a higher likelihood of secondary headaches compared to their younger counterparts [5]. The International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD)-3 attributes secondary headaches to a causative disorder such as vascular, inflammatory, traumatic, and neoplastic aetiologias [6]. However, other causes such as medication-overuse headache should also be recognized as one study has shown that it outnumbers all other causes and can result in significant morbidity if inadequately treated [7]. Early recognition of secondary headaches is critical, as in many cases, early treatment proves lifesaving. A secondary headache may have the characteristics of a primary headache but still fulfil criteria for causation by another disorder [6]. The ICHD-3 defines secondary headaches as: * • Headache attributed to trauma or injury to the head and/or neck * • Headache attributed to cranial or cervical vascular disorder * • Headache attributed to non-vascular intracranial disorder * • Headache attributed to a substance or its withdrawal * • Headache attributed to infection * • Headache attributed to disorder of homoeostasis * • Headache or facial pain attributed to disorder of the cranium, neck, eyes, ears, nose, sinuses, teeth, mouth or other facial or cervical structure * • Headache attributed to psychiatric disorder Only a selected group of secondary headache syndromes will be reviewed in this paper. So-called “red-flags” have been defined to guide the clinician when to consider a secondary headache that may be a symptom of potentially life-threatening disorder. These red flags are rarely based on evidence and will be briefly discussed at the end of the manuscript. Recently, “green flags” have been suggested to help the clinician to recognize frequently “benign” primary headaches, a concept that needs further study. 2. Post- Traumatic Headaches (PTH) The ICHD-3 defines Post Traumatic Headaches (PTH) related to trauma to the head and/or neck as traumatic, whiplash or related to craniotomy [6]. It is classified as acute if it occurs within one week following the inciting event or after reemergence of consciousness or after cessation of medications that would impair discernment or reporting of headache, while persistent PTH is considered if it lasts more than three months [6,8]. While most headaches resolved within this time frame, various reports document an incidence of persistence up to one year from 21 to 54% [9]. Factors associated with PTH include the number of post-traumatic symptoms, young age and female sex [10]. Among patients who developed PTH following war combats, other factors which may be contributory to persistence include various socio-economic factors, insomnia, post-traumatic stress disorder and history of loss of consciousness [11]. It is thought that PTH is likely due to traumatic brain injury (TBI)-induced diffused axonal damage, which culminates in the structural remodeling of various regions involved in pain modulation (somatosensory cortical and subcortical regions, the insular cortex and fiber tracts from relevant cortical and subcortical regions to brainstem nuclei) [12,13]. TBI may also cause PTH by altering brain metabolism. Neuronal injury leads to increased glutamate release along with ion and calcium concentration changes (and associated metabolic abnormalities and oxidative stress). Pharmacologic therapies are nonspecific and may have significant adverse effects – further investigation is needed to support these interventions. fetched_contents.text: Migraine and stroke Migraines have not been shown to cause stroke, but if you have migraine with aura, you have a very slightly higher risk of stroke What is migraine? A migraine attack can have a wide range of symptoms. For many people, the key symptom is a moderate or severe headache. Typically, this is felt as a throbbing pain which gets worse with movement or physical activity. The pain is usually on one side of the head, but it can be all over the head, often with one side worse than the other. The headache is often accompanied by other symptoms such as nausea or vomiting and sensitivity to light, sound or smells. Symptoms in adults can last from around four hours to several days. You may also feel very tired before and after an attack. Migraine attacks tend to start gradually. Many people feel unwell before the onset of the migraine attack, sometimes a few hours or days before the headache itself. Symptoms ahead of a migraine can include changes in mood and energy levels, excessive yawning and aches and pains. These are called prodromal or premonitory symptoms. Some people have several migraines a week. Others may have years between migraine attacks. ---------------------------------------- On this page: The main types of migraine What is the link between migraine and stroke? What causes a migraine? Migraine diagnosis and treatment Where to get help and information Accessible resources ---------------------------------------- Who is affected by migraine? Migraine affects around 12% of men, and up to 33% of women. People of all ages are affected by migraine, but the condition often begins in young adulthood and sometimes improves as you get older. The main types of migraine There are three main subtypes of migraine: migraine without aura, migraine with aura and migraine aura without headache. Symptoms like paralysis, sudden sight loss, difficulty with speech and vertigo (a feeling of the room spinning around you) can be signs of a stroke. If you have any of these symptoms and you have not been diagnosed with migraine, or are unsure if migraine is causing your symptoms, you should call 999. Migraine without aura Up to 80% of people with migraine have this type, which is sometimes called common migraine. It consists of a moderate or severe, throbbing headache with other symptoms, such as nausea and sensitivity to light, sound or smell. The other symptoms usually begin at the same time as the headache and disappear once the headache goes. Many people feel irritable and need to rest in a quiet, dark room or sleep. Migraine with aura Up to a third of people with migraine have migraine with aura (sometimes called classical migraine). Some people have both migraine with aura and without aura at different times. Attacks typically begin with an ‘aura’ consisting of one or more of the following symptoms which develop gradually over about five minutes and last up to an hour. The headache can occur with or after the aura. Types of aura * Visual changes. This is the most common aura symptom. The changes can include flashing lights, zig-zags, sparks or blank spots. These can appear on one side or centrally and commonly expand and move across your field of vision. Visual changes such as flashing lights can also be signs of acute eye disease, so if you get any of these symptoms and migraine has not been diagnosed as the cause, contact your optician or GP urgently. * Sensations such as pins and needles, tingling or numbness, weakness or a spinning sensation (vertigo). * Difficulty speaking. Migraine aura without headache Also known as a silent migraine, this is an aura without the headache. Rare types of migraine There are some rare types of migraine, which are also classed as migraine with aura. Previously known as basilar-type migraine, people with this condition experience two or more of the following symptoms before or with typical migraine symptoms: * Visual disturbances, including double vision (diplopia). * Speaking difficulties (dysarthria). * Hearing problems, including ringing in the ears (tinnitus). * Being unsteady while walking. * Vertigo (a spinning sensation). * Temporary decreased level of consciousness. Hemiplegia means paralysis on one side of the body, and weakness or paralysis on one side is a key symptom of this type of migraine. Other symptoms might include: * Visual problems. * Confusion. * Speech problems. * Dizziness or vertigo (a spinning sensation). These problems usually go away within 24 hours, but they may last a few days. A headache usually follows, though it can occur before these symptoms. If you have a parent with hemiplegic migraines, then you have about a 50% chance of having this type of migraine yourself. This is known as familial hemiplegic migraine (FHM). In some families with FHM, problems have been found with particular genes which affect how the brain cells communicate with each other. Others with no family history may experience hemiplegic migraine. This is known as sporadic hemiplegic migraine. What is the link between migraine and stroke? The relationship between migraine and stroke is complex. Stroke and migraine both happen in the brain. Sometimes the symptoms of a migraine can mimic a stroke, and they may share some underlying risk factors. However, the causes of the symptoms are different. A stroke is due to damage to the blood supply inside the brain, but migraine is thought to be due to problems with brain activity affecting nerves, chemicals and blood vessels in the brain. In a stroke, the blood supply to part of the brain is cut off, killing brain cells. This causes permanent damage to the brain, and can have long-lasting physical, cognitive and emotional effects. A migraine causes pain and sensory disturbances, but these are temporary. The most important diagnoses to consider for sudden severe headaches with visual symptoms are **migraine with aura**, **transient ischemic attack (TIA)**, **subarachnoid hemorrhage**, and **stroke mimics** such as **functional neurological disorder** or **seizure**. The evidence here is strongest for migraine aura, TIA, and stroke-related red flags, while the “stroke mimic” literature emphasizes that transient neurological symptoms can also be mimicked by migraine, seizure, syncope, or functional disorders [N2-R1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

### Common and serious conditions
The evidence points to a few broad categories of conditions. The **most common** is **migraine with aura**, especially because the search results repeatedly describe aura as a sudden, focal visual or sensory phenomenon that can precede or accompany a headache [N2-R1][N2-F2][N2-R3]. The **most serious** conditions are those that represent **secondary headaches or acute stroke/TIA**, including **subarachnoid hemorrhage**, **stroke**, **TIA**, **arterial ischemic stroke**, and **cerebral venous sinus thrombosis** [N1-F1][N3-R4][N4-F4][N6-R3]. The **stroke mimic** literature also notes that migraine aura, seizure, syncope, and functional disorders can mimic stroke [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

### How each diagnosis explains the headache and visual changes
- **Migraine with aura**: The evidence says aura symptoms typically begin with an “aura” of visual changes, such as flashing lights, zig-zags, sparks, or blank spots, which develop gradually over about 5 minutes and last up to an hour [N2-F2]. The headache may follow the aura or occur separately, and the visual symptoms are described as sudden and temporary [N2-R5]. In the stroke association text, visual changes like flashing lights are explicitly labeled as possible signs of acute eye disease, which is why they should prompt urgent GP or optician contact if migraine is not already diagnosed [N2-F2]. This makes migraine a plausible explanation for sudden visual symptoms and a severe headache that comes with them.
- **TIA**: The evidence frames TIA as a warning sign of cerebral infarction and notes that visual symptoms can be part of the transient neurological syndrome [N2-R1][N3-R1][N3-R2]. It also says that TIA symptoms can mimic stroke and that migraine can mimic stroke, so the two are clinically difficult to distinguish [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. In the red-flags literature, sudden onset, high pain intensity, and focal neurological signs are red flags for secondary headaches, including stroke/TIA [N1-R1][N1-F1].
- **Subarachnoid hemorrhage**: This is explicitly called a life-threatening emergency, with the “worst-ever thunderclap headache” as a classic red flag [N1-R4]. While the provided evidence does not detail its exact visual symptoms, it is clearly a serious condition that needs immediate evaluation because it is a brain bleed [N1-R4].
- **Stroke and arterial ischemic stroke**: The evidence notes that transient neurological symptoms can include visual loss, speech difficulties, and focal signs, and that arterial ischemic stroke is one of the secondary headache causes linked with transient neurological symptoms [N3-R4][N1-F1]. The red-flags literature also says that sudden onset, high pain intensity, focal neurological signs, or seizure can point to a secondary headache [N1-R1][N1-F1].
- **Stroke mimics**: The evidence explicitly says migraine aura, seizure, syncope, and functional neurological disorder are common stroke mimics [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. This is important because it shows that the visual symptoms and headache may not be caused by a true vascular event, but by a non-vascular condition.

### Benign versus serious
The evidence supports a clear distinction:
- **Benign/more common**: Migraine with aura is the most common explanation for sudden visual symptoms and associated severe headache, especially if the symptoms are transient, focal, and not associated with other red flags [N2-F2][N2-R5][N3-R1].
- **Serious/urgent**: Subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke, TIA, arterial ischemic stroke, and other secondary headaches are serious and require urgent evaluation [N1-R4][N1-F1][N3-R4][N6-R3]. The red-flags literature emphasizes that sudden onset, high intensity, focal neurological signs, systemic signs, or changes from a preexisting headache are red flags for secondary headaches [N1-R1][N1-F1].

### Bottom line on the mechanism branch
The most likely explanation for sudden severe headaches with visual symptoms is **migraine with aura**, but **stroke/TIA/subarachnoid hemorrhage** must be ruled out because they are serious and potentially life-threatening [N2-F2][N1-R4][N1-F1][N6-R3]. The evidence also shows that the headache and visual changes can be explained by a benign primary headache or by a true vascular emergency, which is why the triage and diagnostic approach must be careful and urgent [N2-R5][N3-R1][N6-R5].

urgency and immediate action branch

The urgency level depends on whether the symptoms suggest a **secondary headache or life-threatening emergency**. The evidence is strongest for red flags, sudden onset, focal neurological signs, and systemic signs, all of which point toward **urgent evaluation** [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The evidence also says that headache severity, sudden onset, and neurological symptoms such as confusion, slurred speech, weakness, numbness, fever, stiff neck, or vision changes are critical red flags that should prompt emergency care [N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-R5].

### Which symptoms suggest life-threatening causes and need immediate evaluation
The most concerning symptoms that strongly suggest immediate evaluation are:
- **Sudden, severe headache** [N1-R4]
- **Vision changes**, especially sudden visual loss or visual disturbances [N1-R2][N2-F2]
- **Confusion**, slurred speech, or other focal neurological signs [N1-R2][N1-R3]
- **Weakness, numbness, or focal deficits** [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Systemic signs** such as fever, stiff neck, or other abnormal signs [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Red flags** such as sudden onset, high pain intensity, or focal neurological signs [N1-R1][N1-F1]

These symptoms are not merely “worrisome”; they are **red flags for secondary headaches, stroke, TIA, or subarachnoid hemorrhage** [N1-F1][N1-R4]. The red-flags source explicitly says that failure to recognize these syndromes can worsen morbidity and mortality, and that clinicians should use red flags to suspect secondary headaches [N1-F1].

### When to call emergency services versus schedule an urgent outpatient appointment
- **Emergency services** are needed if the patient has **any of the red flags listed above**, especially sudden severe headache, vision changes, confusion, or focal neurological signs [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. The evidence also says that headache is an emergency if it is **sudden, severe, and accompanied by neurological symptoms such as confusion or slurred speech** [N1-R2][N1-R3]. In other words, **if the symptoms are acute and could represent a stroke, TIA, or subarachnoid hemorrhage, emergency care is appropriate**.
- **Urgent outpatient appointment** would only be appropriate if the symptoms are **not sudden**, are **mild**, and do not include focal neurological signs or other red flags [N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct cutoff for “non-urgent” outpatient management in this specific scenario, so the safest default is to treat any sudden severe headache with visual changes as **urgent**.

### What clinical history and exam findings matter most for triage
The most important history and exam findings are:
- **Onset pattern**: sudden versus gradual onset, and whether the headache reaches maximal severity quickly [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Duration and frequency**: whether the headache is brief, recurrent, or new [N5-R5]
- **Associated symptoms**: nausea, vomiting, light/sound sensitivity, weakness, numbness, confusion, slurred speech, fever, stiff neck, or visual changes [N1-F1][N2-F2]
- **Focal neurological signs**: visual loss, visual disturbances, speech disturbance, weakness, or other localized deficits [N1-F1][N3-R1][N6-R3]
- **Red flags**: sudden onset, high pain intensity, focal neurological signs, systemic signs, or change from a preexisting headache [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Aura or prodrome**: presence of aura or prodromal symptoms may suggest migraine but must be interpreted carefully in the context of other red flags [N2-F2][N5-R5]

The evidence also emphasizes that headache diagnosis is largely based on criteria and clinical features, not biomarkers [N5-R1], and that frequency, location, duration, triggers, and presence of aura help differentiate primary from secondary headaches [N5-R5]. So the triage should focus on whether the symptoms are consistent with a benign primary headache or whether they point toward a serious secondary syndrome.

### Bottom line on the urgency branch
If the patient has **sudden severe headaches** plus **vision changes** or **focal neurological symptoms**, **emergency evaluation is needed immediately** [N1-R4][N1-R2][N1-R3]. If the symptoms are **mild, not sudden, and without red flags**, an urgent outpatient appointment may be sufficient, but the evidence here strongly supports treating this combination as **urgent** rather than non-urgent. The key triage question is whether the headache and visual symptoms are consistent with a benign migraine or with a life-threatening condition such as stroke, TIA, or subarachnoid hemorrhage [N2-F2][N1-F1][N1-R4].

diagnostic approach and next steps branch

The diagnostic approach should be guided by the **likelihood of a benign primary headache versus a serious secondary headache**, and by the **urgency of the clinical situation**. The evidence supports a stepwise approach: first assess whether the presentation is **urgent**, then use the most appropriate imaging and laboratory tests to rule out life-threatening causes, and finally use history and clinical features to guide the interpretation and next steps [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R5].

### What tests or imaging are typically used in this clinical scenario
The evidence is strongest for **imaging in sudden severe headache** and for **distinguishing primary from secondary headaches**. The imaging guideline excerpt explicitly lists **CT head with and without IV contrast, CTA head with IV contrast, MRA head with IV contrast, MRI head with IV contrast, and MRV head with IV contrast** as initial imaging options for sudden onset severe headache [N4-F4]. However, it also notes that **normal neurologic examination** is the usual initial finding for primary migraine or tension-type headache, and that imaging is not typically required for benign headaches [N4-F4].

In this case, the most relevant initial tests are:
- **Head CT with IV contrast** or **head CT without IV contrast**, depending on the likelihood of bleeding or acute stroke [N4-F4]
- **MRI brain** if the clinical picture is more suggestive of a non-bleeding cause such as TIA, migraine, or a rare secondary headache [N4-F4]
- **MRV** if venous sinus thrombosis is suspected, because the evidence notes that cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is one of the secondary headache causes associated with transient neurological symptoms [N3-R4][N4-F4]
- **Lumbar puncture** may be considered if the headache is thunderclap-like and the CT is normal, especially to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage [N1-F1][N1-R4]

The evidence also notes that headache diagnosis is largely based on criteria and self-reported features, not biomarkers [N5-R1], so imaging should be interpreted alongside the clinical context.

### How to interpret the results and decide on further workup
The interpretation of imaging depends on what the scan shows:
- If **CT or MRI is normal** and the neurologic exam is normal, the likelihood of a serious secondary headache is lower, and the diagnosis may shift toward **benign migraine with aura** or another primary headache disorder [N4-F4][N5-R5]
- If **CT or MRI shows evidence of bleeding, infarction, or other acute lesion**, then the diagnosis is clearly secondary and requires immediate intervention [N1-F1][N4-F4]
- If **venous sinus involvement is seen**, then **cerebral venous sinus thrombosis** must be considered and managed accordingly [N3-R4][N4-F4]
- If the scan is normal but the patient has persistent symptoms, further workup may include **lumbar puncture**, **EEG**, **neuroimaging repeat**, or evaluation for **stroke mimics** such as migraine, seizure, or functional neurological disorder [N1-F1][N6-R5]

The evidence also emphasizes that **headache is often benign** in primary care, but that failure to recognize secondary headaches can worsen outcomes [N1-F1]. So the interpretation should balance the likelihood of a benign migraine with the need to exclude serious pathology.

### What patient education should accompany the next steps
The evidence supports clear patient education because the distinction between benign and serious causes is central to the clinical picture. Patients should be told:
- That **sudden severe headaches with vision changes are not normal** and should be treated as **urgent** if they are sudden, severe, or accompanied by focal neurological symptoms [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4]
- That **migraine with aura** can cause sudden visual symptoms and a severe headache, but that it still requires careful evaluation to rule out stroke/TIA or subarachnoid hemorrhage [N2-F2][N1-F1]
- That **imaging may be needed** to rule out serious causes, and that the results will guide whether further tests or urgent treatment are needed [N4-F4]
- That **if the headache is benign**, lifestyle and trigger management, rest, and follow-up may be sufficient [N5-R5]
- That **if the headache is serious**, emergency evaluation is necessary because some causes can be life-threatening [N1-R4][N1-F1]

The evidence also notes that headache diagnosis is based on criteria and history, not biomarkers [N5-R1], so patients should be encouraged to keep a symptom diary and report any changes in frequency, duration, or associated features [N5-R4]. This helps clinicians distinguish between primary and secondary headaches and guides the next steps.

### Bottom line on the diagnostic approach
The best diagnostic approach is to first assess urgency, then perform appropriate imaging to rule out life-threatening causes such as subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke, or venous sinus thrombosis, and finally interpret the results in the context of history, exam, and headache characteristics [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R5]. Patient education should emphasize that sudden severe headaches with visual changes require serious evaluation, but that many such episodes are benign if the clinical picture is consistent with migraine [N2-F2][N1-R4].

The key point is that **transient neurological symptoms can mimic stroke**, and that the most common mimics include **migraine aura, seizure, syncope, and functional neurological disorder** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The evidence also explicitly says that **TIA is an acute episode of temporary neurological symptoms** and that stroke mimics commonly confound the clinical diagnosis of stroke [N6-R3][N6-R5]. This is important because it shows that the patient’s symptoms may not be caused by a true vascular event, but by a different condition.

### Key features of transient ischemic attack and stroke mimics
- **Transient ischemic attack**: The evidence describes TIA as an **acute episode of temporary neurological symptoms** and notes that it is a warning sign of cerebral infarction [N6-R3]. In the stroke mimic literature, TIA is presented as one of the common mimics, meaning that the clinical picture can resemble stroke even though it is not a true infarction [N6-R5].
- **Stroke mimics**: The evidence lists several common mimics, including **migraine aura, seizure, syncope, functional neurological disorder, and toxic/metabolic changes** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The stroke-manual source also says that the most common mimics are **seizures (20%)**, and that migraine is a common mimic [N6-R2][N6-R5].

### How to differentiate migraine aura from transient ischemic attack
The evidence emphasizes that migraine and TIA are clinically difficult to distinguish at first, and that migraine can mimic stroke while TIA can mimic stroke as well [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The key differentiators in the evidence are:
- **Aura characteristics**: Migraine aura typically begins with **visual changes** such as flashing lights, zig-zags, sparks, or blank spots, which develop gradually over about 5 minutes and last up to an hour [N2-F2]. This is a hallmark of migraine aura and distinguishes it from acute stroke symptoms.
- **Focal neurological signs**: Stroke/TIA often presents with focal signs such as weakness, numbness, speech disturbance, or visual loss, while migraine aura is usually **focal but not necessarily associated with permanent focal deficits** [N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **Time course**: Migraine aura is **transient** and usually resolves within an hour, whereas TIA symptoms are also transient but can last minutes to hours [N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **History and context**: Migraine with aura is often preceded by **prodromal symptoms**, and the headache may follow the aura [N2-F2]. In contrast, TIA and stroke typically do not have this prodrome and are more likely to be preceded by vascular risk factors or a sudden event [N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **Imaging findings**: CT or MRI can help differentiate the two. If imaging shows no acute infarction, a migraine aura is more likely than TIA; if imaging shows evidence of ischemia, stroke/TIA is more likely [N4-F4][N6-R3].

The stroke association text also notes that migraine aura can mimic stroke and that stroke can mimic migraine, which reinforces the need for careful history and examination before imaging [N2-F2]. In other words, the clinical picture alone is often not enough to distinguish the two, and imaging must be used judiciously.

### What clinical clues support urgent vascular evaluation
The evidence supports urgent vascular evaluation when the patient has:
- **Sudden onset** of neurological symptoms [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Focal neurological signs**, such as visual loss, speech disturbance, weakness, or numbness [N1-F1][N6-R3][N6-R5]
- **Systemic signs** such as fever, stiff neck, or other abnormal signs [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Red flags** such as sudden severe headache, high pain intensity, or change from a preexisting headache [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Transient neurological symptoms** that are **not clearly explained by migraine aura** [N6-R5]

In this patient’s case, the presence of **sudden severe headaches** and **vision changes** strongly supports urgent vascular evaluation because those are red flags for secondary headaches and stroke/TIA [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-F1]. The evidence also says that **stroke mimics commonly confound the clinical diagnosis of stroke**, so even if the symptoms look like stroke, they may not represent a true vascular event [N6-R3][N6-R5].

### Bottom line on the stroke mimic branch
The most important message is that **transient neurological symptoms can mimic stroke, and migraine aura is a common mimic** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The evidence supports a careful distinction between migraine and TIA based on the **aura pattern, time course, and accompanying neurological signs**, while also emphasizing that sudden severe headaches and visual changes are red flags that require urgent evaluation [N2-F2][N1-F1][N1-R4]. The key clinical clues supporting urgent vascular evaluation are **sudden onset, focal neurological signs, and red flags** [N1-R1][N1-F1].

2. **Stroke/TIA/subarachnoid hemorrhage** are the serious conditions that must be ruled out because they are life-threatening. The evidence says that sudden severe headache is a classic red flag for subarachnoid hemorrhage and that sudden onset, high pain intensity, and focal neurological signs are red flags for secondary headaches [N1-R4][N1-R1][N1-F1]. The stroke mimic literature also notes that transient neurological symptoms can mimic stroke, so the visual loss and headache may be caused by a true vascular event [N6-R1][N6-R3].

## What makes some conditions more serious
- **Serious/urgent**: Stroke, TIA, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and other secondary headaches are serious because they can cause permanent brain damage or be life-threatening [N1-F1][N1-R4]. The evidence also says that failure to recognize these syndromes can worsen morbidity and mortality [N1-F1].
- **Benign/more common**: Migraine with aura is more common and is generally benign if the clinical picture is consistent with migraine and no serious red flags are present [N2-F2][N2-R5][N5-R5]. However, migraine should still be evaluated carefully because it can mimic stroke and may coexist with vascular risk factors [N2-F2][N6-R5].

## What the symptoms mean in more detail
- **Sudden severe headache**: This is the most urgent signal. The evidence calls sudden, severe headache a red flag and describes thunderclap headaches as classic for subarachnoid hemorrhage [N1-R4][N1-R1].
- **Visual loss in one eye**: This is concerning because sudden visual loss can be a sign of stroke, TIA, or other acute neurological conditions [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The stroke mimic literature also notes that transient neurological symptoms such as visual loss can mimic stroke [N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **Short duration**: The fact that the headache lasts only a few hours is not reassuring on its own, because some serious conditions such as TIA or migraine can also have brief episodes [N1-R1][N2-F2].

## When to call emergency services versus schedule an urgent outpatient appointment
- **Call emergency services immediately** if you have **any of the red flags**, especially sudden severe headache, vision changes, confusion, slurred speech, weakness, numbness, fever, stiff neck, or focal neurological signs [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R1][N1-F1]. This is especially important if the headache is **sudden, severe, and accompanied by neurological symptoms** [N1-R2][N1-R3].
- **Schedule an urgent outpatient appointment** only if the symptoms are mild, not sudden, and do not include focal neurological signs or other red flags [N1-F1]. But in your case, because the symptoms are sudden and include vision changes, the safest default is to treat them as **urgent** rather than non-urgent [N1-R4][N1-F1].

## What the doctor will likely do
The diagnostic approach will depend on how urgent the situation is. The evidence supports a stepwise approach:
- First, **assess urgency** based on sudden onset, severity, and neurological symptoms [N1-R1][N1-F1].
- Then, use appropriate **imaging** such as **CT head with IV contrast**, **MRI brain**, or **MRV** if venous sinus thrombosis is suspected, because sudden severe headache with visual symptoms may require imaging to rule out serious causes [N4-F4][N3-R4].
- If the imaging is normal and the neurological exam is normal, the diagnosis may shift toward **benign migraine** or another primary headache disorder [N4-F4][N5-R5].
- If the scan shows evidence of bleeding, infarction, or other acute lesion, the diagnosis is clearly secondary and requires urgent intervention [N1-F1][N4-F4].

## How to interpret the results
- **Normal imaging** with no acute lesion usually makes a serious vascular cause less likely, but it does not rule out migraine or other benign conditions [N4-F4][N5-R5].
- **Abnormal imaging** showing bleeding, infarction, or other acute changes means a serious cause is present and requires immediate action [N1-F1][N4-F4].
- If the scan is normal but the symptoms persist or recur, further workup may include **lumbar puncture**, **EEG**, or evaluation for **stroke mimics** such as migraine, seizure, or functional neurological disorder [N1-F1][N6-R5].

## What patient education should accompany the next steps
The evidence supports clear patient education because the distinction between benign and serious causes is central. Patients should understand that:
- **Sudden severe headaches with vision changes are not normal** and should be treated as **urgent** if they are sudden, severe, or accompanied by focal neurological symptoms [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4].
- **Migraine with aura** can cause sudden visual symptoms and a severe headache, but it still requires careful evaluation to rule out stroke/TIA or subarachnoid hemorrhage [N2-F2][N1-F1].
- **Imaging may be needed** to rule out serious causes, and the results will guide whether further tests or urgent treatment are needed [N4-F4].
- If the headache is **benign**, lifestyle and trigger management, rest, and follow-up may be sufficient [N5-R5].
- If the headache is **serious**, emergency evaluation is necessary because some causes can be life-threatening [N1-R4][N1-F1].

## Bottom line
Yes, you should be concerned enough to seek urgent medical evaluation. Sudden severe headaches with visual loss in one eye are red flags for **stroke, TIA, or subarachnoid hemorrhage**, but **migraine with aura** is also a plausible explanation. Because these symptoms can be serious, the best course of action is to **seek immediate care** rather than waiting [N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-F2][N6-R3]. The doctor will assess how urgent the situation is, use appropriate imaging if needed, and decide whether the symptoms are likely benign or require urgent treatment [N4-F4][N5-R5].

## If you want, I can also help you understand what to tell your doctor
If you decide to visit a doctor, you can say something like:
- “I have been having sudden, severe headaches that last a few hours, and sometimes I have trouble seeing clearly out of one eye.”
- “I want to make sure this is not a serious condition like stroke or subarachnoid hemorrhage.”
- “I’ve heard that migraine can also cause visual symptoms, so I want to know if that’s a possibility.”

This will help the doctor quickly understand the main concerns and guide the next steps [N2-F2][N1-F1][N4-F4].

The most important diagnoses to consider for sudden severe headaches with visual symptoms are **migraine with aura**, **transient ischemic attack (TIA)**, **subarachnoid hemorrhage**, and **stroke mimics** such as **functional neurological disorder** or **seizure**. The evidence here is strongest for migraine aura, TIA, and stroke-related red flags, while the “stroke mimic” literature emphasizes that transient neurological symptoms can also be mimicked by migraine, seizure, syncope, or functional disorders [N2-R1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

### Common and serious conditions
The evidence points to a few broad categories of conditions. The **most common** is **migraine with aura**, especially because the search results repeatedly describe aura as a sudden, focal visual or sensory phenomenon that can precede or accompany a headache [N2-R1][N2-F2][N2-R3]. The **most serious** conditions are those that represent **secondary headaches or acute stroke/TIA**, including **subarachnoid hemorrhage**, **stroke**, **TIA**, **arterial ischemic stroke**, and **cerebral venous sinus thrombosis** [N1-F1][N3-R4][N4-F4][N6-R3]. The **stroke mimic** literature also notes that migraine aura, seizure, syncope, and functional disorders can mimic stroke [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

### How each diagnosis explains the headache and visual changes
- **Migraine with aura**: The evidence says aura symptoms typically begin with an “aura” of visual changes, such as flashing lights, zig-zags, sparks, or blank spots, which develop gradually over about 5 minutes and last up to an hour [N2-F2]. The headache may follow the aura or occur separately, and the visual symptoms are described as sudden and temporary [N2-R5]. In the stroke association text, visual changes like flashing lights are explicitly labeled as possible signs of acute eye disease, which is why they should prompt urgent GP or optician contact if migraine is not already diagnosed [N2-F2]. This makes migraine a plausible explanation for sudden visual symptoms and a severe headache that comes with them.
- **TIA**: The evidence frames TIA as a warning sign of cerebral infarction and notes that visual symptoms can be part of the transient neurological syndrome [N2-R1][N3-R1][N3-R2]. It also says that TIA symptoms can mimic stroke and that migraine can mimic stroke, so the two are clinically difficult to distinguish [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. In the red-flags literature, sudden onset, high pain intensity, and focal neurological signs are red flags for secondary headaches, including stroke/TIA [N1-R1][N1-F1].
- **Subarachnoid hemorrhage**: This is explicitly called a life-threatening emergency, with the “worst-ever thunderclap headache” as a classic red flag [N1-R4]. While the provided evidence does not detail its exact visual symptoms, it is clearly a serious condition that needs immediate evaluation because it is a brain bleed [N1-R4].
- **Stroke and arterial ischemic stroke**: The evidence notes that transient neurological symptoms can include visual loss, speech difficulties, and focal signs, and that arterial ischemic stroke is one of the secondary headache causes linked with transient neurological symptoms [N3-R4][N1-F1]. The red-flags literature also says that sudden onset, high pain intensity, focal neurological signs, or seizure can point to a secondary headache [N1-R1][N1-F1].
- **Stroke mimics**: The evidence explicitly says migraine aura, seizure, syncope, and functional neurological disorder are common stroke mimics [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. This is important because it shows that the visual symptoms and headache may not be caused by a true vascular event, but by a non-vascular condition.

### Benign versus serious
The evidence supports a clear distinction:
- **Benign/more common**: Migraine with aura is the most common explanation for sudden visual symptoms and associated severe headache, especially if the symptoms are transient, focal, and not associated with other red flags [N2-F2][N2-R5][N3-R1].
- **Serious/urgent**: Subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke, TIA, arterial ischemic stroke, and other secondary headaches are serious and require urgent evaluation [N1-R4][N1-F1][N3-R4][N6-R3]. The red-flags literature emphasizes that sudden onset, high intensity, focal neurological signs, systemic signs, or changes from a preexisting headache are red flags for secondary headaches [N1-R1][N1-F1].

### Bottom line on the mechanism branch
The most likely explanation for sudden severe headaches with visual symptoms is **migraine with aura**, but **stroke/TIA/subarachnoid hemorrhage** must be ruled out because they are serious and potentially life-threatening [N2-F2][N1-R4][N1-F1][N6-R3]. The evidence also shows that the headache and visual changes can be explained by a benign primary headache or by a true vascular emergency, which is why the triage and diagnostic approach must be careful and urgent [N2-R5][N3-R1][N6-R5].

The urgency level depends on whether the symptoms suggest a **secondary headache or life-threatening emergency**. The evidence is strongest for red flags, sudden onset, focal neurological signs, and systemic signs, all of which point toward **urgent evaluation** [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The evidence also says that headache severity, sudden onset, and neurological symptoms such as confusion, slurred speech, weakness, numbness, fever, stiff neck, or vision changes are critical red flags that should prompt emergency care [N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-R5].

### Which symptoms suggest life-threatening causes and need immediate evaluation
The most concerning symptoms that strongly suggest immediate evaluation are:
- **Sudden, severe headache** [N1-R4]
- **Vision changes**, especially sudden visual loss or visual disturbances [N1-R2][N2-F2]
- **Confusion**, slurred speech, or other focal neurological signs [N1-R2][N1-R3]
- **Weakness, numbness, or focal deficits** [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Systemic signs** such as fever, stiff neck, or other abnormal signs [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Red flags** such as sudden onset, high pain intensity, or focal neurological signs [N1-R1][N1-F1]

These symptoms are not merely “worrisome”; they are **red flags for secondary headaches, stroke, TIA, or subarachnoid hemorrhage** [N1-F1][N1-R4]. The red-flags source explicitly says that failure to recognize these syndromes can worsen morbidity and mortality, and that clinicians should use red flags to suspect secondary headaches [N1-F1].

### When to call emergency services versus schedule an urgent outpatient appointment
- **Emergency services** are needed if the patient has **any of the red flags listed above**, especially sudden severe headache, vision changes, confusion, or focal neurological signs [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. The evidence also says that headache is an emergency if it is **sudden, severe, and accompanied by neurological symptoms such as confusion or slurred speech** [N1-R2][N1-R3]. In other words, **if the symptoms are acute and could represent a stroke, TIA, or subarachnoid hemorrhage, emergency care is appropriate**.
- **Urgent outpatient appointment** would only be appropriate if the symptoms are **not sudden**, are **mild**, and do not include focal neurological signs or other red flags [N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct cutoff for “non-urgent” outpatient management in this specific scenario, so the safest default is to treat any sudden severe headache with visual changes as **urgent**.

### What clinical history and exam findings matter most for triage
The most important history and exam findings are:
- **Onset pattern**: sudden versus gradual onset, and whether the headache reaches maximal severity quickly [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Duration and frequency**: whether the headache is brief, recurrent, or new [N5-R5]
- **Associated symptoms**: nausea, vomiting, light/sound sensitivity, weakness, numbness, confusion, slurred speech, fever, stiff neck, or visual changes [N1-F1][N2-F2]
- **Focal neurological signs**: visual loss, visual disturbances, speech disturbance, weakness, or other localized deficits [N1-F1][N3-R1][N6-R3]
- **Red flags**: sudden onset, high pain intensity, focal neurological signs, systemic signs, or change from a preexisting headache [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Aura or prodrome**: presence of aura or prodromal symptoms may suggest migraine but must be interpreted carefully in the context of other red flags [N2-F2][N5-R5]

The evidence also emphasizes that headache diagnosis is largely based on criteria and clinical features, not biomarkers [N5-R1], and that frequency, location, duration, triggers, and presence of aura help differentiate primary from secondary headaches [N5-R5]. So the triage should focus on whether the symptoms are consistent with a benign primary headache or whether they point toward a serious secondary syndrome.

### Bottom line on the urgency branch
If the patient has **sudden severe headaches** plus **vision changes** or **focal neurological symptoms**, **emergency evaluation is needed immediately** [N1-R4][N1-R2][N1-R3]. If the symptoms are **mild, not sudden, and without red flags**, an urgent outpatient appointment may be sufficient, but the evidence here strongly supports treating this combination as **urgent** rather than non-urgent. The key triage question is whether the headache and visual symptoms are consistent with a benign migraine or with a life-threatening condition such as stroke, TIA, or subarachnoid hemorrhage [N2-F2][N1-F1][N1-R4].

- **Sudden, severe headache** [N1-R4]
- **Vision changes**, especially sudden visual loss or visual disturbances [N1-R2][N2-F2]
- **Confusion**, slurred speech, or other focal neurological signs [N1-R2][N1-R3]

- **Systemic signs** such as fever, stiff neck, or other abnormal signs [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Red flags** such as sudden onset, high pain intensity, or focal neurological signs [N1-R1][N1-F1]

- **Emergency services** are needed if the patient has **any of the red flags listed above**, especially sudden severe headache, vision changes, confusion, or focal neurological signs [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. The evidence also says that headache is an emergency if it is **sudden, severe, and accompanied by neurological symptoms such as confusion or slurred speech** [N1-R2][N1-R3]. The most important history and exam findings are:
- **Onset pattern**: sudden versus gradual onset, and whether the headache reaches maximal severity quickly [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Duration and frequency**: whether the headache is brief, recurrent, or new [N5-R5]
- **Associated symptoms**: nausea, vomiting, light/sound sensitivity, weakness, numbness, confusion, slurred speech, fever, stiff neck, or visual changes [N1-F1][N2-F2]
- **Focal neurological signs**: visual loss, visual disturbances, speech disturbance, weakness, or other localized deficits [N1-F1][N3-R1][N6-R3]
- **Red flags**: sudden onset, high pain intensity, focal neurological signs, systemic signs, or change from a preexisting headache [N1-R1][N1-F1]

### Bottom line on the urgency branch
If the patient has **sudden severe headaches** plus **vision changes** or **focal neurological symptoms**, **emergency evaluation is needed immediately** [N1-R4][N1-R2][N1-R3]. If the symptoms are **mild, not sudden, and without red flags**, an urgent outpatient appointment may be sufficient, but the evidence here strongly supports treating this combination as **urgent** rather than non-urgent. diagnostic approach and next steps branch

The diagnostic approach should be guided by the **likelihood of a benign primary headache versus a serious secondary headache**, and by the **urgency of the clinical situation**. The evidence supports a stepwise approach: first assess whether the presentation is **urgent**, then use the most appropriate imaging and laboratory tests to rule out life-threatening causes, and finally use history and clinical features to guide the interpretation and next steps [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R5].

### What tests or imaging are typically used in this clinical scenario
The evidence is strongest for **imaging in sudden severe headache** and for **distinguishing primary from secondary headaches**. The imaging guideline excerpt explicitly lists **CT head with and without IV contrast, CTA head with IV contrast, MRA head with IV contrast, MRI head with IV contrast, and MRV head with IV contrast** as initial imaging options for sudden onset severe headache [N4-F4]. However, it also notes that **normal neurologic examination** is the usual initial finding for primary migraine or tension-type headache, and that imaging is not typically required for benign headaches [N4-F4].

In this case, the most relevant initial tests are:
- **Head CT with IV contrast** or **head CT without IV contrast**, depending on the likelihood of bleeding or acute stroke [N4-F4]
- **MRI brain** if the clinical picture is more suggestive of a non-bleeding cause such as TIA, migraine, or a rare secondary headache [N4-F4]
- **MRV** if venous sinus thrombosis is suspected, because the evidence notes that cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is one of the secondary headache causes associated with transient neurological symptoms [N3-R4][N4-F4]
- **Lumbar puncture** may be considered if the headache is thunderclap-like and the CT is normal, especially to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage [N1-F1][N1-R4]

The evidence also notes that headache diagnosis is largely based on criteria and self-reported features, not biomarkers [N5-R1], so imaging should be interpreted alongside the clinical context.

### How to interpret the results and decide on further workup
The interpretation of imaging depends on what the scan shows:
- If **CT or MRI is normal** and the neurologic exam is normal, the likelihood of a serious secondary headache is lower, and the diagnosis may shift toward **benign migraine with aura** or another primary headache disorder [N4-F4][N5-R5]
- If **CT or MRI shows evidence of bleeding, infarction, or other acute lesion**, then the diagnosis is clearly secondary and requires immediate intervention [N1-F1][N4-F4]
- If **venous sinus involvement is seen**, then **cerebral venous sinus thrombosis** must be considered and managed accordingly [N3-R4][N4-F4]
- If the scan is normal but the patient has persistent symptoms, further workup may include **lumbar puncture**, **EEG**, **neuroimaging repeat**, or evaluation for **stroke mimics** such as migraine, seizure, or functional neurological disorder [N1-F1][N6-R5]

The evidence also emphasizes that **headache is often benign** in primary care, but that failure to recognize secondary headaches can worsen outcomes [N1-F1]. So the interpretation should balance the likelihood of a benign migraine with the need to exclude serious pathology.

### What patient education should accompany the next steps
The evidence supports clear patient education because the distinction between benign and serious causes is central to the clinical picture. Patients should be told:
- That **sudden severe headaches with vision changes are not normal** and should be treated as **urgent** if they are sudden, severe, or accompanied by focal neurological symptoms [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4]
- That **migraine with aura** can cause sudden visual symptoms and a severe headache, but that it still requires careful evaluation to rule out stroke/TIA or subarachnoid hemorrhage [N2-F2][N1-F1]
- That **imaging may be needed** to rule out serious causes, and that the results will guide whether further tests or urgent treatment are needed [N4-F4]
- That **if the headache is benign**, lifestyle and trigger management, rest, and follow-up may be sufficient [N5-R5]
- That **if the headache is serious**, emergency evaluation is necessary because some causes can be life-threatening [N1-R4][N1-F1]

The evidence also notes that headache diagnosis is based on criteria and history, not biomarkers [N5-R1], so patients should be encouraged to keep a symptom diary and report any changes in frequency, duration, or associated features [N5-R4]. This helps clinicians distinguish between primary and secondary headaches and guides the next steps.

### Bottom line on the diagnostic approach
The best diagnostic approach is to first assess urgency, then perform appropriate imaging to rule out life-threatening causes such as subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke, or venous sinus thrombosis, and finally interpret the results in the context of history, exam, and headache characteristics [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R5]. Patient education should emphasize that sudden severe headaches with visual changes require serious evaluation, but that many such episodes are benign if the clinical picture is consistent with migraine [N2-F2][N1-R4].

The key point is that **transient neurological symptoms can mimic stroke**, and that the most common mimics include **migraine aura, seizure, syncope, and functional neurological disorder** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The evidence also explicitly says that **TIA is an acute episode of temporary neurological symptoms** and that stroke mimics commonly confound the clinical diagnosis of stroke [N6-R3][N6-R5]. This is important because it shows that the patient’s symptoms may not be caused by a true vascular event, but by a different condition.

### Key features of transient ischemic attack and stroke mimics
- **Transient ischemic attack**: The evidence describes TIA as an **acute episode of temporary neurological symptoms** and notes that it is a warning sign of cerebral infarction [N6-R3]. In the stroke mimic literature, TIA is presented as one of the common mimics, meaning that the clinical picture can resemble stroke even though it is not a true infarction [N6-R5].
- **Stroke mimics**: The evidence lists several common mimics, including **migraine aura, seizure, syncope, functional neurological disorder, and toxic/metabolic changes** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The stroke-manual source also says that the most common mimics are **seizures (20%)**, and that migraine is a common mimic [N6-R2][N6-R5].

### How to differentiate migraine aura from transient ischemic attack
The evidence emphasizes that migraine and TIA are clinically difficult to distinguish at first, and that migraine can mimic stroke while TIA can mimic stroke as well [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The key differentiators in the evidence are:
- **Aura characteristics**: Migraine aura typically begins with **visual changes** such as flashing lights, zig-zags, sparks, or blank spots, which develop gradually over about 5 minutes and last up to an hour [N2-F2]. This is a hallmark of migraine aura and distinguishes it from acute stroke symptoms.
- **Focal neurological signs**: Stroke/TIA often presents with focal signs such as weakness, numbness, speech disturbance, or visual loss, while migraine aura is usually **focal but not necessarily associated with permanent focal deficits** [N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **Time course**: Migraine aura is **transient** and usually resolves within an hour, whereas TIA symptoms are also transient but can last minutes to hours [N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **History and context**: Migraine with aura is often preceded by **prodromal symptoms**, and the headache may follow the aura [N2-F2]. In contrast, TIA and stroke typically do not have this prodrome and are more likely to be preceded by vascular risk factors or a sudden event [N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **Imaging findings**: CT or MRI can help differentiate the two. If imaging shows no acute infarction, a migraine aura is more likely than TIA; if imaging shows evidence of ischemia, stroke/TIA is more likely [N4-F4][N6-R3].

The stroke association text also notes that migraine aura can mimic stroke and that stroke can mimic migraine, which reinforces the need for careful history and examination before imaging [N2-F2]. In other words, the clinical picture alone is often not enough to distinguish the two, and imaging must be used judiciously.

### What clinical clues support urgent vascular evaluation
The evidence supports urgent vascular evaluation when the patient has:
- **Sudden onset** of neurological symptoms [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Focal neurological signs**, such as visual loss, speech disturbance, weakness, or numbness [N1-F1][N6-R3][N6-R5]
- **Systemic signs** such as fever, stiff neck, or other abnormal signs [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Red flags** such as sudden severe headache, high pain intensity, or change from a preexisting headache [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Transient neurological symptoms** that are **not clearly explained by migraine aura** [N6-R5]

In this patient’s case, the presence of **sudden severe headaches** and **vision changes** strongly supports urgent vascular evaluation because those are red flags for secondary headaches and stroke/TIA [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-F1]. The evidence also says that **stroke mimics commonly confound the clinical diagnosis of stroke**, so even if the symptoms look like stroke, they may not represent a true vascular event [N6-R3][N6-R5].

### Bottom line on the stroke mimic branch
The most important message is that **transient neurological symptoms can mimic stroke, and migraine aura is a common mimic** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The evidence supports a careful distinction between migraine and TIA based on the **aura pattern, time course, and accompanying neurological signs**, while also emphasizing that sudden severe headaches and visual changes are red flags that require urgent evaluation [N2-F2][N1-F1][N1-R4]. The key clinical clues supporting urgent vascular evaluation are **sudden onset, focal neurological signs, and red flags** [N1-R1][N1-F1].

The most concerning symptoms that strongly suggest immediate evaluation are:
- **Sudden, severe headache** [N1-R4]
- **Vision changes**, especially sudden visual loss or visual disturbances [N1-R2][N2-F2]

The red-flags source explicitly says that failure to recognize these syndromes can worsen morbidity and mortality, and that clinicians should use red flags to suspect secondary headaches [N1-F1].

- **Emergency services** are needed if the patient has **any of the red flags listed above**, especially sudden severe headache, vision changes, confusion, or focal neurological signs [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. The evidence also says that headache is an emergency if it is **sudden, severe, and accompanied by neurological symptoms such as confusion or slurred speech** [N1-R2][N1-R3]. In other words, **if the symptoms are acute and could represent a stroke, TIA, or subarachnoid hemorrhage, emergency care is appropriate**.
- **Urgent outpatient appointment** would only be appropriate if the symptoms are **not sudden**, are **mild**, and do not include focal neurological signs or other red flags [N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct cutoff for “non-urgent” outpatient management in this specific scenario, so the safest default is to treat any sudden severe headache with visual changes as **urgent**.

### What clinical history and exam findings matter most for triage
The most important history and exam findings are:
- **Onset pattern**: sudden versus gradual onset, and whether the headache reaches maximal severity quickly [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Duration and frequency**: whether the headache is brief, recurrent, or new [N5-R5]
- **Associated symptoms**: nausea, vomiting, light/sound sensitivity, weakness, numbness, confusion, slurred speech, fever, stiff neck, or visual changes [N1-F1][N2-F2]
- **Focal neurological signs**: visual loss, visual disturbances, speech disturbance, weakness, or other localized deficits [N1-F1][N3-R1][N6-R3]
- **Red flags**: sudden onset, high pain intensity, focal neurological signs, systemic signs, or change from a preexisting headache [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Aura or prodrome**: presence of aura or prodromal symptoms may suggest migraine but must be interpreted carefully in the context of other red flags [N2-F2][N5-R5]

The evidence also emphasizes that headache diagnosis is largely based on criteria and clinical features, not biomarkers [N5-R1], and that frequency, location, duration, triggers, and presence of aura help differentiate primary from secondary headaches [N5-R5]. So the triage should focus on whether the symptoms are consistent with a benign primary headache or whether they point toward a serious secondary syndrome.

### Bottom line on the urgency branch
If the patient has **sudden severe headaches** plus **vision changes** or **focal neurological symptoms**, **emergency evaluation is needed immediately** [N1-R4][N1-R2][N1-R3]. If the symptoms are **mild, not sudden, and without red flags**, an urgent outpatient appointment may be sufficient, but the evidence here strongly supports treating this combination as **urgent** rather than non-urgent. The key triage question is whether the headache and visual symptoms are consistent with a benign migraine or with a life-threatening condition such as stroke, TIA, or subarachnoid hemorrhage [N2-F2][N1-F1][N1-R4].

The diagnostic approach should be guided by the **likelihood of a benign primary headache versus a serious secondary headache**, and by the **urgency of the clinical situation**. The evidence supports a stepwise approach: first assess whether the presentation is **urgent**, then use the most appropriate imaging and laboratory tests to rule out life-threatening causes, and finally use history and clinical features to guide the interpretation and next steps [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R5].

### What tests or imaging are typically used in this clinical scenario
The evidence is strongest for **imaging in sudden severe headache** and for **distinguishing primary from secondary headaches**. The imaging guideline excerpt explicitly lists **CT head with and without IV contrast, CTA head with IV contrast, MRA head with IV contrast, MRI head with IV contrast, and MRV head with IV contrast** as initial imaging options for sudden onset severe headache [N4-F4]. However, it also notes that **normal neurologic examination** is the usual initial finding for primary migraine or tension-type headache, and that imaging is not typically required for benign headaches [N4-F4].

In this case, the most relevant initial tests are:
- **Head CT with IV contrast** or **head CT without IV contrast**, depending on the likelihood of bleeding or acute stroke [N4-F4]
- **MRI brain** if the clinical picture is more suggestive of a non-bleeding cause such as TIA, migraine, or a rare secondary headache [N4-F4]
- **MRV** if venous sinus thrombosis is suspected, because the evidence notes that cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is one of the secondary headache causes associated with transient neurological symptoms [N3-R4][N4-F4]
- **Lumbar puncture** may be considered if the headache is thunderclap-like and the CT is normal, especially to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage [N1-F1][N1-R4]

The evidence also notes that headache diagnosis is largely based on criteria and self-reported features, not biomarkers [N5-R1], so imaging should be interpreted alongside the clinical context.

### How to interpret the results and decide on further workup
The interpretation of imaging depends on what the scan shows:
- If **CT or MRI is normal** and the neurologic exam is normal, the likelihood of a serious secondary headache is lower, and the diagnosis may shift toward **benign migraine with aura** or another primary headache disorder [N4-F4][N5-R5]
- If **CT or MRI shows evidence of bleeding, infarction, or other acute lesion**, then the diagnosis is clearly secondary and requires immediate intervention [N1-F1][N4-F4]
- If **venous sinus involvement is seen**, then **cerebral venous sinus thrombosis** must be considered and managed accordingly [N3-R4][N4-F4]
- If the scan is normal but the patient has persistent symptoms, further workup may include **lumbar puncture**, **EEG**, **neuroimaging repeat**, or evaluation for **stroke mimics** such as migraine, seizure, or functional neurological disorder [N1-F1][N6-R5]

The evidence also emphasizes that **headache is often benign** in primary care, but that failure to recognize secondary headaches can worsen outcomes [N1-F1]. So the interpretation should balance the likelihood of a benign migraine with the need to exclude serious pathology.

### What patient education should accompany the next steps
The evidence supports clear patient education because the distinction between benign and serious causes is central to the clinical picture. Patients should be told:
- That **sudden severe headaches with vision changes are not normal** and should be treated as **urgent** if they are sudden, severe, or accompanied by focal neurological symptoms [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4]
- That **migraine with aura** can cause sudden visual symptoms and a severe headache, but that it still requires careful evaluation to rule out stroke/TIA or subarachnoid hemorrhage [N2-F2][N1-F1]
- That **imaging may be needed** to rule out serious causes, and that the results will guide whether further tests or urgent treatment are needed [N4-F4]
- That **if the headache is benign**, lifestyle and trigger management, rest, and follow-up may be sufficient [N5-R5]
- That **if the headache is serious**, emergency evaluation is necessary because some causes can be life-threatening [N1-R4][N1-F1]

The evidence also notes that headache diagnosis is based on criteria and history, not biomarkers [N5-R1], so patients should be encouraged to keep a symptom diary and report any changes in frequency, duration, or associated features [N5-R4]. This helps clinicians distinguish between primary and secondary headaches and guides the next steps.

### Bottom line on the diagnostic approach
The best diagnostic approach is to first assess urgency, then perform appropriate imaging to rule out life-threatening causes such as subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke, or venous sinus thrombosis, and finally interpret the results in the context of history, exam, and headache characteristics [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R5]. Patient education should emphasize that sudden severe headaches with visual changes require serious evaluation, but that many such episodes are benign if the clinical picture is consistent with migraine [N2-F2][N1-R4].

### Key features of transient ischemic attack and stroke mimics
- **Transient ischemic attack**: The evidence describes TIA as an **acute episode of temporary neurological symptoms** and notes that it is a warning sign of cerebral infarction [N6-R3]. In the stroke mimic literature, TIA is presented as one of the common mimics, meaning that the clinical picture can resemble stroke even though it is not a true infarction [N6-R5].
- **Stroke mimics**: The evidence lists several common mimics, including **migraine aura, seizure, syncope, functional neurological disorder, and toxic/metabolic changes** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The stroke-manual source also says that the most common mimics are **seizures (20%)**, and that migraine is a common mimic [N6-R2][N6-R5].

### How to differentiate migraine aura from transient ischemic attack
The evidence emphasizes that migraine and TIA are clinically difficult to distinguish at first, and that migraine can mimic stroke while TIA can mimic stroke as well [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The key differentiators in the evidence are:
- **Aura characteristics**: Migraine aura typically begins with **visual changes** such as flashing lights, zig-zags, sparks, or blank spots, which develop gradually over about 5 minutes and last up to an hour [N2-F2]. This is a hallmark of migraine aura and distinguishes it from acute stroke symptoms.
- **Focal neurological signs**: Stroke/TIA often presents with focal signs such as weakness, numbness, speech disturbance, or visual loss, while migraine aura is usually **focal but not necessarily associated with permanent focal deficits** [N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **Time course**: Migraine aura is **transient** and usually resolves within an hour, whereas TIA symptoms are also transient but can last minutes to hours [N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **History and context**: Migraine with aura is often preceded by **prodromal symptoms**, and the headache may follow the aura [N2-F2]. In contrast, TIA and stroke typically do not have this prodrome and are more likely to be preceded by vascular risk factors or a sudden event [N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **Imaging findings**: CT or MRI can help differentiate the two. If imaging shows no acute infarction, a migraine aura is more likely than TIA; if imaging shows evidence of ischemia, stroke/TIA is more likely [N4-F4][N6-R3].

The stroke association text also notes that migraine aura can mimic stroke and that stroke can mimic migraine, which reinforces the need for careful history and examination before imaging [N2-F2]. In other words, the clinical picture alone is often not enough to distinguish the two, and imaging must be used judiciously.

### What clinical clues support urgent vascular evaluation
The evidence supports urgent vascular evaluation when the patient has:
- **Sudden onset** of neurological symptoms [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Focal neurological signs**, such as visual loss, speech disturbance, weakness, or numbness [N1-F1][N6-R3][N6-R5]
- **Systemic signs** such as fever, stiff neck, or other abnormal signs [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Red flags** such as sudden severe headache, high pain intensity, or change from a preexisting headache [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Transient neurological symptoms** that are **not clearly explained by migraine aura** [N6-R5]

In this patient’s case, the presence of **sudden severe headaches** and **vision changes** strongly supports urgent vascular evaluation because those are red flags for secondary headaches and stroke/TIA [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-F1]. The evidence also says that **stroke mimics commonly confound the clinical diagnosis of stroke**, so even if the symptoms look like stroke, they may not represent a true vascular event [N6-R3][N6-R5].

### Bottom line on the stroke mimic branch
The most important message is that **transient neurological symptoms can mimic stroke, and migraine aura is a common mimic** [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The evidence supports a careful distinction between migraine and TIA based on the **aura pattern, time course, and accompanying neurological signs**, while also emphasizing that sudden severe headaches and visual changes are red flags that require urgent evaluation [N2-F2][N1-F1][N1-R4]. The key clinical clues supporting urgent vascular evaluation are **sudden onset, focal neurological signs, and red flags** [N1-R1][N1-F1].

# Final integrated answer to the patient

## Short answer
Yes, you should be **concerned enough to seek urgent medical evaluation**. Sudden severe headaches that last for a few hours, especially when accompanied by **vision changes in one eye**, are red flags that may point to a serious condition such as **stroke, transient ischemic attack (TIA), or subarachnoid hemorrhage**. However, **migraine with aura** is also a plausible explanation, so it’s important not to ignore the symptoms and to get them checked promptly [N2-F2][N1-F1][N1-R4].

## Why this matters
The evidence shows that **sudden severe headaches** are not normal and should be evaluated carefully because they can be the first sign of a serious brain problem [N1-R4][N1-F1]. The key red flags include sudden onset, high pain intensity, focal neurological signs, systemic signs, or changes from a preexisting headache [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In your case, the fact that the headaches are **sudden, severe, and sometimes associated with visual loss in one eye** fits several red flags and should not be treated lightly [N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-F2].

## Most likely explanations
The evidence points to two main possibilities:
1. **Migraine with aura** is the most common explanation for sudden visual symptoms and associated severe headache. Aura can include sudden visual changes such as flashing lights, zig-zags, sparks, or blank spots that develop gradually and may last up to an hour [N2-F2]. In the stroke association text, these visual symptoms are explicitly labeled as possible signs of acute eye disease and should prompt urgent GP or optician contact if migraine is not already diagnosed [N2-F2].
2. **Stroke/TIA/subarachnoid hemorrhage** are the serious conditions that must be ruled out because they are life-threatening. The evidence says that sudden severe headache is a classic red flag for subarachnoid hemorrhage and that sudden onset, high pain intensity, and focal neurological signs are red flags for secondary headaches [N1-R4][N1-R1][N1-F1]. The stroke mimic literature also notes that transient neurological symptoms can mimic stroke, so the visual loss and headache may be caused by a true vascular event [N6-R1][N6-R3].

## What makes some conditions more serious
- **Serious/urgent**: Stroke, TIA, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and other secondary headaches are serious because they can cause permanent brain damage or be life-threatening [N1-F1][N1-R4]. The evidence also says that failure to recognize these syndromes can worsen morbidity and mortality [N1-F1].
- **Benign/more common**: Migraine with aura is more common and is generally benign if the clinical picture is consistent with migraine and no serious red flags are present [N2-F2][N2-R5][N5-R5]. However, migraine should still be evaluated carefully because it can mimic stroke and may coexist with vascular risk factors [N2-F2][N6-R5].

## What the symptoms mean in more detail
- **Sudden severe headache**: This is the most urgent signal. The evidence calls sudden, severe headache a red flag and describes thunderclap headaches as classic for subarachnoid hemorrhage [N1-R4][N1-R1].
- **Visual loss in one eye**: This is concerning because sudden visual loss can be a sign of stroke, TIA, or other acute neurological conditions [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The stroke mimic literature also notes that transient neurological symptoms such as visual loss can mimic stroke [N6-R3][N6-R5].
- **Short duration**: The fact that the headache lasts only a few hours is not reassuring on its own, because some serious conditions such as TIA or migraine can also have brief episodes [N1-R1][N2-F2].

## When to call emergency services versus schedule an urgent outpatient appointment
- **Call emergency services immediately** if you have **any of the red flags**, especially sudden severe headache, vision changes, confusion, slurred speech, weakness, numbness, fever, stiff neck, or focal neurological signs [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R1][N1-F1]. This is especially important if the headache is **sudden, severe, and accompanied by neurological symptoms** [N1-R2][N1-R3].
- **Schedule an urgent outpatient appointment** only if the symptoms are mild, not sudden, and do not include focal neurological signs or other red flags [N1-F1]. But in your case, because the symptoms are sudden and include vision changes, the safest default is to treat them as **urgent** rather than non-urgent [N1-R4][N1-F1].

## What the doctor will likely do
The diagnostic approach will depend on how urgent the situation is. The evidence supports a stepwise approach:
- First, **assess urgency** based on sudden onset, severity, and neurological symptoms [N1-R1][N1-F1].
- Then, use appropriate **imaging** such as **CT head with IV contrast**, **MRI brain**, or **MRV** if venous sinus thrombosis is suspected, because sudden severe headache with visual symptoms may require imaging to rule out serious causes [N4-F4][N3-R4].
- If the imaging is normal and the neurological exam is normal, the diagnosis may shift toward **benign migraine** or another primary headache disorder [N4-F4][N5-R5].
- If the scan shows evidence of bleeding, infarction, or other acute lesion, the diagnosis is clearly secondary and requires urgent intervention [N1-F1][N4-F4].

## How to interpret the results
- **Normal imaging** with no acute lesion usually makes a serious vascular cause less likely, but it does not rule out migraine or other benign conditions [N4-F4][N5-R5].
- **Abnormal imaging** showing bleeding, infarction, or other acute changes means a serious cause is present and requires immediate action [N1-F1][N4-F4].
- If the scan is normal but the symptoms persist or recur, further workup may include **lumbar puncture**, **EEG**, or evaluation for **stroke mimics** such as migraine, seizure, or functional neurological disorder [N1-F1][N6-R5].

## What patient education should accompany the next steps
The evidence supports clear patient education because the distinction between benign and serious causes is central. Patients should understand that:
- **Sudden severe headaches with vision changes are not normal** and should be treated as **urgent** if they are sudden, severe, or accompanied by focal neurological symptoms [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4].
- **Migraine with aura** can cause sudden visual symptoms and a severe headache, but it still requires careful evaluation to rule out stroke/TIA or subarachnoid hemorrhage [N2-F2][N1-F1].
- **Imaging may be needed** to rule out serious causes, and the results will guide whether further tests or urgent treatment are needed [N4-F4].
- If the headache is **benign**, lifestyle and trigger management, rest, and follow-up may be sufficient [N5-R5].
- If the headache is **serious**, emergency evaluation is necessary because some causes can be life-threatening [N1-R4][N1-F1].

## Bottom line
Yes, you should be concerned enough to seek urgent medical evaluation. Sudden severe headaches with visual loss in one eye are red flags for **stroke, TIA, or subarachnoid hemorrhage**, but **migraine with aura** is also a plausible explanation. Because these symptoms can be serious, the best course of action is to **seek immediate care** rather than waiting [N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-F2][N6-R3]. The doctor will assess how urgent the situation is, use appropriate imaging if needed, and decide whether the symptoms are likely benign or require urgent treatment [N4-F4][N5-R5].

## If you want, I can also help you understand what to tell your doctor
If you decide to visit a doctor, you can say something like:
- “I have been having sudden, severe headaches that last a few hours, and sometimes I have trouble seeing clearly out of one eye.”
- “I want to make sure this is not a serious condition like stroke or subarachnoid hemorrhage.”
- “I’ve heard that migraine can also cause visual symptoms, so I want to know if that’s a possibility.”

This will help the doctor quickly understand the main concerns and guide the next steps [N2-F2][N1-F1][N4-F4].
